newsitem.title: USA: US TREASURIES LITTLE CHANGED BEFORE 30-YR AUCTION.
newsitem.headline: US TREASURIES LITTLE CHANGED BEFORE 30-YR AUCTION.

text.p: U.S. government securities prices were little changed at midday, an hour before the bidding deadline for the last leg of the Treasury's three-part quarterly refinancing effort.
The Treasury will sell $10.0 billion in 30-year bonds at 1300 EDT/1700 GMT.
On Tuesday, the Treasury sold $16.0 billion in three-year notes. On Wednesday, it sold $12.0 billion in 10-year notes.
The 30-year bonds to be sold at 1300 EDT/1700 GMT yielded 6.445 percent in when-issued trade at 1220 EDT/1620 GMT.

The market opened on a firm note and was apparently not affected by the government's report that jobless claims in the latest week rose to 300,000 from a revised 275,000 a week earlier. Economists had forecast an average of 307,000 new claims in a Reuters poll.
Some dealer purchases in the cash bond were said to aid the market toward mid-morning. Session highs were reached shortly before 1000 EDT/1400 GMT.
Then the government reported an unexpectedly sharp 1.9 percent jump in June wholesale inventories.
Analysts at Standard & Poor's MMS said that jump could lead to a higher number for second-quarter revised GDP (Gross Domestic Product) than they had been expecting.
David Sloan, senior economist at I.D.E.A., said the June inventory number was well above expectations.
"Some people will ask if this will detract from third-quarter growth," Sloan added. "But this shows inventories making a long overdue catchup with sales rather than rising to uncomfortable levels."
Sloan said sales have risen by 5.4 percent year over year while inventories have risen by just 3.0 percent.
The bond market seemed to pay little attention to the Challenger, Gray report showing that U.S. layoffs more than tripled in July from their June levels.

The moderate gains achieved by mid-morning were erased by midday as players adjusted positions ahead of the Treasury auction and the market built in a somewhat more enticing yield on the 30-year bonds to be sold in that process.

Elliott Platt, managing director and director of economic research at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette, said he was "a little bit surprised" at how well the market had bounced back from losses incurred on Friday and Monday.
"I thought we'd get a little more followthrough on Friday's deterioriation but starting yesterday, we seem to have had a rejuvenation of buying interest," he said.
Platt said it was "impressive" that the 30-year bond yield could not be pushed through 6.50 percent. He said the market's action is reflective of general global liquidity.
"There are plenty of funds out there for investment," he said.
But he expressed some concern about the 30-year auction.
"We might be setting ourselves up for a very sloppy auction if the price concession isn't great enough," he said.
Platt said the market could hit a bump next week if the July retail sales and industrial production come in strong.

"I'm a little worried about the retail sales and industrial production (numbers)," he said. "We're forecasting 0.7 percent for retail sales with the non-auto component up 0.5 percent. And we're estimating industrial production probably to be up around 0.5 percent.
"The market conceivably could be upset about what it sees in the retail sales and industrial production data," he said.
At the short end of the maturity range, three- and six-month bill rates were each up one basis point to 5.15 percent and 5.20 percent, respectively. Year bill rates were unchanged at 5.22 percent.
The two-year Treasury note was unchanged at 99-30/32, yielding 5.91 percent.
The five-year note was up 2/32 to 99-20/32 to yield 6.09 percent.
Ten-year notes were priced at 99-16/32, yielding 6.19 percent.
((-- North American Treasury Desk, 212-859-1679 ))
